title: ChatGPT and AI Chatbots in Education: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews, Scoping Reviews, and Meta-Analyses
venue: International Journal of Education and Information Technologies
extended_summary:
This umbrella review examines the rapidly expanding literature on ChatGPT and related large language model (LLM)-based chatbots in education. Its central purpose is to synthesize evidence from existing systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, bibliometric reviews, narrative reviews, and rapid reviews in order to identify reported benefits, limitations, ethical concerns, and policy implications of these tools in educational settings.

The paper does not study a single intervention with primary participants; instead, it aggregates findings from 41 review studies published between 2023 and 2025. The reviewed literature covers a wide range of contexts, with the strongest concentration in higher education and substantial attention to medicine/health, STEM, and language learning. The review notes that chatbots are typically used for academic writing support, tutoring, feedback, exam preparation, and self-directed learning, mostly in online, blended, or hybrid settings.

The umbrella review concludes that AI chatbots can support personalized learning, learner autonomy, motivation, and some aspects of academic performance, but the evidence base is limited by short-term, exploratory studies and an overreliance on self-reported or observational outcomes. It highlights major safety and quality concerns, especially hallucinations, outdated or inaccurate information, source opacity, overreliance by students, and threats to academic integrity. The authors argue that effective educational use requires stronger policy frameworks, educator professional development, human oversight, and more rigorous longitudinal research.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an umbrella review of 41 systematic/scoping reviews and meta-analyses, so it is peer-reviewed and methodologically structured, but it does not conduct a new meta-analysis of primary studies and explicitly notes that no formal critical appraisal checklist was used. Evidence quality is therefore moderate rather than high.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports important, practice-relevant concerns and some positive effects, but most findings are synthesized qualitatively and lack pooled effect sizes. The impact on K-12 populations is therefore suggestive but unclear, especially because the underlying literature is dominated by higher education rather than school settings.

interventions.use_case: umbrella review of ChatGPT and similar LLM-based chatbots used for tutoring, Q&A, feedback, content generation, and conversational support across education

finding.finding_summary: The review reports broadly positive effects on academic writing, comprehension, and written expression, but also notes risks that AI-generated text can suppress original thinking and critical engagement. The evidence base is mostly drawn from short-term, review-level syntheses rather than new experiments, so no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: writing quality, written expression, comprehension, and academic writing performance across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: Reviews summarized in the umbrella review suggest ChatGPT and similar tools support vocabulary acquisition, speaking practice, and general language development in EFL/ESL contexts. However, the paper emphasizes that robust long-term evidence is limited and that much of the literature is short-term and descriptive.
finding.measure: vocabulary acquisition, speaking fluency, and language development outcomes in EFL/ESL studies

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that LLM chatbots are often used in STEM and health education for problem-solving, concept explanation, and clinical reasoning, with some reviews reporting performance comparable to or better than human learners in narrow tasks such as medical licensing preparation. At the same time, it highlights weaker performance in mathematics and software testing, plus hallucinations and factual inaccuracies in science-heavy domains.
finding.measure: problem-solving, clinical reasoning, exam preparation, and domain-specific accuracy in STEM/medical contexts

finding.finding_summary: Across non-language, non-math domains, the review reports that chatbots can support content understanding, exam preparation, and task completion in areas such as medicine, engineering, law, and professional education. Benefits are described at the review level, but the paper does not provide pooled quantitative effects.
finding.measure: domain-specific learning outcomes in medicine, engineering, law, and other professional/disciplinary contexts

finding.finding_summary: The umbrella review reports increases in motivation, confidence, autonomy, and engagement when students use chatbots for self-paced support and low-stakes practice. It also notes concerns about reduced initiative, overreliance, and shallower engagement when use is unstructured.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, learner autonomy, confidence, and self-paced participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly identifies possible gains in critical thinking, metacognition, creativity, and self-regulated learning, especially when educators provide structured prompts and reflection tasks. It also reports negative or null-like concerns: overreliance may reduce critical thinking and produce shallow, rote use of AI responses.
finding.measure: critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulated learning, creativity, and reflective engagement

finding.finding_summary: Reviews synthesized in the paper consistently describe productivity benefits for both students and educators, including faster feedback, content generation, grading support, and reduced routine workload. The paper does not report pooled quantitative effects, but the direction of evidence is strongly favorable for efficiency-related tasks.
finding.measure: teacher workload, feedback turnaround, content generation, grading, and task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The umbrella review highlights major institutional concerns around academic integrity, privacy, transparency, policy readiness, and governance for AI in education. It also reports a strong consensus that schools and universities need explicit policy frameworks, but the evidence base is mostly descriptive and review-based rather than outcome-evaluative.
finding.measure: policy, governance, academic integrity, privacy, institutional preparedness, and AI literacy
